extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, judges and legal scholars studying U.S. patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of substantive doctrines governing U.S. patents: nature of patent rights, interplay with state police/taxing powers, remedies, government use, prior user exceptions, territorial scope, and term/foreign-patent limitations. Aimed at explaining legal rules with case citations and statutory references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent rights are property, not harmful monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights are rights of property 'at once dignified, honorable, and strong' and are an 'organized system, with well-settled rules, supporting itself at once by its utility, and by the wealth which it creates and commands.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court views patents as property rather than harmful monopolies; supports treating patents as property in legal analysis and remedies (cites Justice Miller and Merrill v. Yeomans).

rubrics_metrics.name: State power to regulate sale of patent rights (reasonable fraud-protection statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: States may enact reasonable regulations (e.g., requiring filing authenticated copies of letters patent and affidavits) to protect citizens from fraud in sales of patent rights; such statutes are valid if 'a reasonable and fair exercise' to check a known evil and prevent fraud and imposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kansas statute requiring filing and oath upheld (Allen v. Riley). Expense of filing and affidavits not oppressive or unreasonable. States retain fair latitude to legislate unless Congress has displaced them by legislation; federal assignment/record provisions do not automatically preempt all state regulation of patent transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State police, taxing, and regulatory powers apply to patented things
rubrics_metrics.description: Every State can regulate making, selling, and using patented things to the same extent it lawfully regulates unpatented things; patented things are subject to common-carrier law, revenue laws, and police powers (e.g., compelled impartial service in public businesses; state taxes; regulation of manufacture/storage/sale of dangerous substances; medical practice laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: telephone business may be compelled to serve all; patentees still subject to state taxes (sewing-machine example); local authorities can regulate manufacture/storage of dynamite, poisons, explosive oils; patent does not authorize practicing medicine contrary to state medical-practice laws; patent on gambling devices does not protect against state prosecution for gambling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold nature of patentee's rights (tangible-use right vs. exclusionary federal right)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee has (1) a right to make, use, and sell specimens of the invented thing (a right subject to state police and taxing powers) and (2) a federal right to prevent others from making, using, or selling (the exclusionary right, which exists by virtue of federal patent laws and is largely beyond state control except in exercise of police powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishing these two rights explains why states can regulate the physical articles but cannot generally interfere with the federal exclusionary monopoly; use this framework when analyzing conflicts between state regulation and federal patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents as intangible property and remedies in equity (creditor's bill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights, as intangible property, cannot be seized and sold under common-law execution writs, but they can be reached by a creditor's bill in equity and applied to pay the owner's debts (similar to trusts, choses in action, or stock).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity courts can decree payment, or order sale of the patent right, require assignment execution by debtor, or appoint a trustee/master in chancery to effect assignment (cases cited: Newton v. Buck; Ager v. Murray; Wilson v. Fire Alarm Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use and 1910 compensation statute (Court of Claims remedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior rule: government had no greater right than private citizens to make/use patented inventions without license. The 1910 Act provides that when the United States uses a patented invention without license or lawful right, the patentee may recover reasonable compensation in the Court of Claims, subject to exclusions (e.g., claims based on articles formerly owned/used by the U.S.; claims by patentees who are government employees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute allows the U.S. to appropriate a license under eminent-domain-like principles (Crozier v. Krupp). The United States may plead any defenses available in infringement actions. An injunction against government officers is displaced where the U.S. has appropriated the right; the appropriate remedy is an action in the Court of Claims as provided by the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractors supplying the government and injunction immunity (Marconi)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor who supplies the government with articles that would be infringing if supplied to a private party may be immune from injunction (Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. v. Simon), on the theory the contractor supplies goods to a lawful licensee (the government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The holding has been interpreted to preclude injunctions against contractors; it is debated whether the contractor remains liable for damages and profits. Treat with caution: some cases hold damages/profits recoverable; policy considerations noted regarding fairness to patentees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user/purchase exemption for tangible specimens (Revised Statutes §4899)
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent covers any use or sale of any specimen of the patented thing which was purchased of the inventor, or made by another with his knowledge and consent, before his application for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to tangible machines/articles (not processes). The word 'person' is interpreted broadly (not restricted to privity by purchase). If applicant submitted device plans to federal government to obtain bids and the successful bidder had consent, no injunction will issue even after patent issuance. Willful obstructive interference delaying issuance may defeat damages claims. Case examples: Sub-Target Gun Co. v. Hollifield Target Practice Rod Co.; Federal Construction Co. v. Park Improvement Co.; Wade v. Metcalf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user exemption does not apply to process patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4899 treats machines or other patentable articles only; a process is a series of acts and is outside the statute. Prior making or practicing of a process before patent application (even innocently or by re-inventor) does not exempt that person from infringement once a process patent issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: a process cannot be purchased or be tangible property; rights to perform acts are not vested property interests protected by §4899. Re-inventors of a process have no special right after a later patent issues to the first inventor. Use this distinction when advising clients about prior use defenses for processes versus machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial scope of U.S. patents (extent and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: A United States patent is generally co-extensive with the territory under U.S. jurisdiction (including tide-waters). U.S. patents cover use in or under tide-waters and extend to the decks of U.S. ships even on the high seas; they do not, however, extend to mere use of the invention on a foreign ship temporarily in a U.S. harbor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: patent on submarine telegraph cable covered use in U.S. jurisdiction waters; but no right to make/use in another's house. Even when Congress grants others exclusive rights to do particular acts (e.g., to lay cables), that grant does not necessarily confer a right to use another's patented articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular patent term and exceptions (general 17-year term; design patents & other special terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular duration of a U.S. patent for a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter is seventeen years from date of issue (Section 4884). 'Every patent' is qualified: design patents and some patents filed under special conditions may have different terms (design patents may be 14, 7, or 3.5 years as elected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note statutory exceptions where duration is otherwise prescribed (e.g., design patents, patents based on prior foreign patents under earlier statutes). Consult statutory text and amendments for patents filed/issued in particular eras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior foreign patents on U.S. patent term (limitation to foreign term in some cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory rule (historical): 'Every patent granted for an invention which has previously been patented in a foreign country shall be so limited as to expire at the same time with the foreign patent...' (applies to certain patents granted after July 8, 1870, on applications filed before Jan. 1, 1898). The rule applies only where the foreign patent was taken out by the U.S. patentee or with his knowledge/consent or by someone in privity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat applicability carefully: subsequent treaty provisions (e.g., Brussels treaty Art. 4 bis) were held not self-executing in some domestic cases (Cameron Septic Tank Co. v. Knoxville), and amendments to statutes changed coverage. Does not apply where the invention was only described (not claimed) in the foreign patent, or where the foreign patent never became operative; may apply where foreign patent granted exclusive right to make but not to use or sell. There is complex case law on whether extensions of foreign patents affect U.S. patent term—depends on whether extensions were possible/absolute under foreign law at relevant times.

rubrics_metrics.name: When foreign patent extensions can affect U.S. patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the foreign patent could be extended under a statute in force when the U.S. application was filed and issued—and that extension power conferred an absolute right—courts have in some cases held that the U.S. patent should not expire with the first term of the foreign patent (i.e., U.S. patent term may be limited to the foreign patent's overall effective period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuit courts diverge: some hold hypothetical/possible extensions under foreign law affect U.S. term even if not actually extended; others hold no effect unless extension was absolute/actually obtained. Termination of foreign patent for noncompliance does not affect corresponding U.S. patent duration. See collection of cases cited in treatise (e.g., Bate Refrigerating Co. v. Hammond and later circuit decisions).
